newsitem.title: USA: Lilly, others in pact for diabetes research.
newsitem.headline: Lilly, others in pact for diabetes research.

text.p: Eli Lilly and Co, Eastern Virginia Medical School and McGill University said Thursday they reached a licensing agreement on the discovery of a gene and its related products that could play a key role in treating diabetes more effectively.

Two research teams have identified a new gene whose products appear to stimulate the regeneration of islet cells, they said in a joint statement. These cells produce insulin in the pancreas and regulate its production to meet the body's demands.

The teams were led by Aaron Vinik M.D., director of the EVMS Diabetes Research Institute and Lawrence Rosenberg M.D., director of the McGill Transplantation Surgery Program and the Centre for Pancreatic Diseases at Montreal General Hospital.

"The critical event in the development of diabetes is a reduction of insulin production in the pancreas. The understanding of mechanisms that promote the differentiation and proliferation of the pancreatic islets, the site of insulin-producing cells, could someday dramatically change the way we prevent and treat diabetes," said Jose Caro M.D., vice president endocrine research for Lilly.

"While our findings are still preliminary and much more research in both animals and humans is needed, the identification of a new gene that influences the number of islet cells could lead to answers to the larger problem of why diabetes develops," said Vinik in a statement.
Under the terms of the agreement, Eastern Virginia Medical School and McGill University will receive initial fees, milestone payments and royalties on potential product sales.
In exchange, Lilly will receive an exclusive license to the gene and its related products and exclusive commercialization rights for any products that result from this agreement.

About 18 million people in the United States and Canada have diabetes, a disease in which the body does not produce or properly use insulin, the hormone required to convert food into energy. Diabetes is the fourth leading cause of death in the United States and Canada.
